record.paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
record.original_question: What is the number of rich words of a given length?

evidence.quote: What is the number of rich words of a given length?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A finite word $w$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ is called *rich* (or *full*) if it contains exactly $|w|+1$ distinct palindromic factors (including the empty word), which is the maximum possible number of distinct palindromic factors of a word of length $|w|$. For an integer $q\ge 2$ and an integer $n\ge 0$, let $R_q(n)$ denote the number of rich words of length $n$ over an alphabet of cardinality $q$.

Determine $R_q(n)$ exactly, i.e., give a closed-form expression (or an exact enumeration formula) for the number of rich words of length $n$ over an alphabet of size $q$. In particular, settle the case $q=2$ of binary rich words.
artifact.category_tag: Combinatorics on words / rich words enumeration
artifact.status_search_result: No exact formula for the number $R_q(n)$ of rich words of length $n$ is known. Only bounds and growth-rate results have been established: it is known that $\lim_{n\to\infty} R_q(n)^{1/n}=1$ (subexponential growth), and a 2025 preprint provides the first explicit subexponential upper bound of the form involving iterated logarithms. A binary upper bound $R_2(n)\le c\cdot 1.605^n$ has also been recorded. The enumeration problem itself remains open.

status_evidence.title: Subexponential upper bound on the number of rich words
status_evidence.snippet: Provides the first explicit subexponential upper bound on R(n); no exact formula is known.
status_evidence.claim: The exact enumeration of rich words remains open; only subexponential upper bounds are available.

status_evidence.title: On the Number of Rich Words
status_evidence.snippet: Establishes that the nth root of R_q(n) tends to 1, i.e. subexponential growth, and binary bound R_n(2) ≤ c·1.605^n.
status_evidence.claim: Growth-rate results are known but no closed-form count.
